intro: “I did lock the door!”, “I do like your dress”, “Do sit down”: in English, you can put do / does / did before an affirmative verb to insist, contradict or show contrast. Said with the right stress, this small word makes spoken English much more natural and expressive.
objectifs: Form the emphatic affirmative: do / does / did + base form.
Use it to contradict, insist, show contrast or confirm an expectation.
Use the emphatic, polite imperative (Do sit down, Do be careful).
Know that with be, auxiliary have and modals, you stress the auxiliary instead of adding do.

texte: In an affirmative sentence in the present simple or past simple, add do, does or did before the base form, exactly as in a question or a negative, but without “not”.
The main verb loses its ending: “She likes” → “She does like”; “I went” → “I did go”. This is the most common mistake.
In speech, do / does / did is always stressed: the stress creates the emphasis. Without stress, the sentence sounds strange.
The most common use: answering a negative statement or a doubt.
You can answer with the full sentence (“I did lock the door!”) or with a short answer with a stressed auxiliary (“I DID!”).
exemples: “You didn't lock the door.” – “I DID lock it! I checked twice.”
“You never listen to me.” – “I DO listen to you!”
“Ama doesn't eat meat.” – “She DOES eat meat. She just doesn't eat pork.”

texte: Do / does / did strengthens a feeling, an opinion or a wish: “I do hope you can come”, “I do apologise for the delay” (a formal apology), “You do look tired.”
It also confirms that something expected really happened: “He said he'd come, and he did come.”
In argumentative writing, it highlights a concession: “This method does have some advantages, but…”.
exemples: I do hope the weather will be nice for the wedding.
We do apologise for any inconvenience.
The plan did work in the end.
Online learning does have advantages, but it can't replace a teacher.

texte: Do / does / did highlights the positive part of a contrast: “I don't eat meat, but I do eat fish.”
Often we contrast what is not true with what is true, or what we don't know with what we do know: “I don't know her name, but I do know where she works.”
exemples: He doesn't speak Dutch, but he does understand it.
I didn't win, but I did enjoy the race.
We don't have much money, but we do have time.

texte: Before an imperative, “do” makes an invitation warmer or a request more urgent: “Do come in!”, “Do help yourself”, “Do be careful”. It sounds slightly formal or British, but very polite.
With “be”, the emphatic imperative also uses “do”: “Do be quiet!”, “Do be careful on the road.” This is the only case where “do” goes before “be”.
“Don't you dare!” (I forbid you to…) and “Do tell me!” (please tell me!) are common expressions.
exemples: Do come in and make yourself at home.
Do help yourself to some more cake.
Do be careful, the roads are icy.

sections.titre: With be, have and modals: stress the auxiliary
texte: When the sentence already contains “be”, an auxiliary (have / has, be + -ing) or a modal (can, will, must…), don't add “do”. Simply say the auxiliary in its full, stressed form, without contraction.
“I'm listening” → “I AM listening!”; “I've finished” → “I HAVE finished!”; “I can swim” → “I CAN swim!”
In informal messages, you can underline or use italics for the auxiliary; in careful writing, adverbs are often better (really, indeed, certainly).

formule: DO / DOES / DID (stressed) + base form · Do + imperative · With be / have / modal: stressed auxiliary (I AM, I HAVE, I CAN)
prononciation: The emphatic auxiliary is always in its full form and strongly stressed: do /duː/, does /dʌz/, did /dɪd/, with a higher, then falling voice.
The verb after it is less stressed: “I DID lock it” /aɪ ˈdɪd lɒk ɪt/.
With be and modals, no contraction: “I AM” /aɪ ˈæm/, “I CAN” /aɪ ˈkæn/ (strong form, although “can” is usually weak /kən/).
In “Do sit down”, the stress falls on “Do” and “sit”; the tone is warm.
Without stress, the emphatic sentence doesn't work: in speech, the intonation carries the meaning.
erreurs: I did went to the meeting.
I did go to the meeting.
With a modal, stress the modal.

dialogue.contexte: In Kigali, Eric and his sister Divine come home after a weekend away and find the house in a mess.
lignes: Eric! The kitchen window is open. You didn't close it before we left!
I did close it! I remember doing it.
Then who opened it? And look, someone has eaten all the bananas.
I don't know who opened the window, but I do know who ate the bananas…
Contrast: don't know… but do know.
Our cousin Patrick! He did say he would come and water the plants.
did say: he really said it.
Ah, that explains it. Well, he did water them. They look great.
You see? I am a responsible brother! Now do sit down, and I'll make some tea.

mots: Don't contradict me in front of the client.
to say the opposite of what someone has said
She insists that she locked the door.
to say firmly that something is true
I assure you that the work is finished.
to tell someone that something is certainly true
It was indeed a difficult year.
I did actually call you yesterday.
She certainly knows how to cook.
Honestly, I did try my best.
used to show you are telling the truth
We do apologise for the delay.
Do help yourself to some food.
to take food or drink without asking

exercices.consigne: Say what do / does / did is used for: contradiction, contrast, polite invitation or strong feeling.
items: “You didn't call me!” – “I did call you, twice!”
I don't like sport, but I do enjoy watching football.
Do come in and sit down.
I do hope you'll be able to come.

exercices.consigne: Complete with do / does / did + the verb in brackets.
items: She doesn't speak Dutch, but she ___ (understand) it.
“Why didn't you tell me?” – “I ___ (tell) you! You weren't listening.”
He ___ (work) hard, even if he's not very fast.
I ___ (enjoy) the concert last night. It was amazing.

exercices.consigne: Contradict each sentence with an emphatic form (watch out for be and modals).
items: I AM listening! (no do with be)
I CAN swim! (no do with a modal)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I did went to the meeting.
I did go to the meeting.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite each sentence with do / does / did to add the emphasis shown in brackets.
items: He doesn't drink alcohol, but he drinks a lot of coffee. (contrast)
He doesn't drink alcohol, but he does drink a lot of coffee.

exercices.consigne: Write a short exchange (4–6 lines) in which someone wrongly accuses you of forgetting something. Defend yourself with at least four different emphatic forms (do, does, did, stressed auxiliary, imperative).
items: A: You forgot to pay the electricity bill! B: I did pay it! I paid it online on Monday. A: Then why does the website say it's unpaid? B: I don't know, but I do have the receipt. Look, here it is. A: Oh… you're right. Sorry. B: No problem. I AM organised sometimes! Now do relax.

a_retenir: do / does / did (stressed) + base form: I do like it, she does speak it, we did lock it.
Uses: contradicting, insisting (I do hope), contrast (I don't…, but I do…), confirming (and he did come).
Warm or urgent imperative: Do sit down, Do help yourself, Do be careful.
With be, auxiliary have and modals: no do; stress the auxiliary (I AM, I HAVE, I CAN).
No ending after do / does / did: does like, did go.
